features.headline: Inside the NRL's $5.3bn deal.
features.descriptor: How the 2028 to 2034 rights deal is carved up

article.standfirst: The NRL's seven-year, $5.3 billion rights deal is the biggest in Australian sport. Here is who gets what.
body: The NRL's new broadcast deal is worth $5.3 billion over seven years, from 2028 to 2034, and it is the biggest commercial agreement any Australian sport has signed. The league says cash per year jumps 90 per cent on the current arrangement. Spread evenly, that is about $757 million a season, against the more than $400 million a year the NRL announced when it signed the 2023 to 2027 deal. By the same rough maths, the AFL's $4.5 billion deal for 2025 to 2031 works out at $643 million a season.

The headline number gets the attention. The structure is where the value sits. There are three buyers and each gets a different slice. Foxtel Group, which is owned by DAZN, stays the home of the league across Foxtel and Kayo Sports. It shows every NRL and NRLW premiership match live, including the finals, other than State of Origin and the grand final.

Nine keeps the free-to-air crown jewels. It has exclusive coverage of the NRL Grand Final and of both the men's and women's State of Origin series. On top of that it simulcasts three NRL and NRLW games a week, so the pay-TV home and the free home show the same match at the same time. For a sponsor, that mix matters. Origin and the grand final deliver the mass audience on free TV, while the weekly simulcasts keep brand exposure steady across the season. Across the Tasman, Sky NZ will put more than 130 fixtures on its free platforms.

Then there is the world outside Australia and New Zealand. Foxtel has a revenue-sharing and marketing agreement on international rights, which excludes New Zealand and Papua New Guinea. Foxtel chief executive Patrick Delany says NRL content will reach 200 international markets through DAZN. ARLC chairman Peter V'landys has described going global as the priority once this deal is done.

The deal also changes who holds the pen. The Australian Rugby League Commission takes back control of season structure, scheduling and the draw. V'landys says that will mean fair scheduling for all clubs. He also says about 95 per cent of the money is cash and only 5 per cent contra, which is free advertising and promotion rather than dollars in the bank.

The growth built into the contract is just as important. Perth joins in 2027 as the 18th team, with the PNG Chiefs following in 2028. The NRL has told DAZN it will look at a 20th club around 2029, with New Zealand and Queensland the names in the frame. If that happens, Foxtel picks up an extra exclusive game each week. More games mean more inventory for sponsors, more reasons for fans to subscribe and more leverage for the league at the next renewal.

The rest of the market was circling. Seven and Amazon Prime Video were reported to have been interested, and Ten has been named too. The NRL went the other way on packaging. It kept a single pay-TV and streaming partner rather than splitting games across several services. NRL chief executive Andrew Abdo said the league could have put more content behind the paywall but went the other way. The open question is price, because fans will want to know if Kayo gets dearer. Delany says the entry-level Kayo price has risen only once in nearly nine years, and V'landys says he has protected the price point.

For brands and rights holders, the message is clear. Free-to-air reach is locked in for Origin and the grand final through 2034, the pay-TV rights are priced for growth, and the league now controls its own calendar. That gives sponsors seven years of certainty on where their logos will be seen, and gives clubs a stronger base to sell from. Nine's chief executive Matt Stanton has pointed to a commitment to bring the action live and free, and the NRL says its audience has roughly doubled over the past five years, so the pitch to brands is built on momentum as well as money. How much of that momentum survives a bigger, more expensive league is the real test.
article.close: Watch the 20th club decision, the Kayo price and whether DAZN can sell the NRL overseas, because those three will decide how the deal ages.

features.headline: The NBA's most expensive square.
features.descriptor: How NBA jersey patches work and what they're worth

article.standfirst: An Australian-founded AI company now owns the priciest bit of fabric in American sport, and it's about six centimetres wide.
body: From this NBA season, IREN's logo sits on the front of every Golden State Warriors jersey. Sportico reported the multi-year deal at more than US$50 million a year, which would make it the biggest sponsorship in North American team sport. IREN began in 2018 as Iris Energy, a Sydney-based bitcoin miner set up by brothers Will and Daniel Roberts, and now trades on Nasdaq as an AI cloud business. It replaces Rakuten, the Warriors' only patch partner until now, and also lands on the Santa Cruz Warriors' jerseys in the G League and the warmup tops of the WNBA's Golden State Valkyries.

So what are they actually buying? The NBA's board of governors signed off on jersey sponsorship in April 2016 as a three-year trial, starting with the 2017-18 season. The rules are tight: one logo, roughly 2.5 inches square, on the front left of the jersey opposite the Nike swoosh. Each club sells its own. The Philadelphia 76ers were first out of the blocks, announcing StubHub in May 2016. Compare that with an AFL or NRL jumper, where sponsors share the front, back and sleeves. The NBA went the other way and sold scarcity. One badge, one brand, on every game, every highlight clip and every replica jersey in the club shop.

Scarcity has done wonders for the price. When the Warriors signed Rakuten in 2017, the three-year, US$60 million deal was the richest in the league. In 2021 the Lakers topped it, signing Korean food brand Bibigo on a five-year deal reported by the LA Times at more than US$100 million. This June IREN's number blew both out of the water, and a month later ESPN reported the Lakers' new patch with finance app Albert at north of US$30 million a year. The trial has long since become a permanent fixture.

The 2026 off-season turned into a full reshuffle. In July the Dallas Mavericks signed JPMorganChase, the bank's first NBA patch, bundled with banking partner rights, a dedicated arena entrance for Chase cardholders and new community courts across North Texas. In September the Milwaukee Bucks swapped Motorola for Uline, a Wisconsin packaging supplier that has backed the club since 2013. The Phoenix Suns replaced PayPal with Paze, the digital wallet run by Early Warning Services, the company behind Zelle. The 76ers replaced Crypto.com with Bloom Energy, adding the Delaware Blue Coats' jerseys and a seven-figure charity investment. And in October Disney extended with the Orlando Magic, where it has been on the jersey since 2017, and added a Walt Disney World Atrium at Kia Center.

Look at who's buying. Blinkfire counted 29 of 30 teams with a patch in 2025-26, and financial brands were the biggest group with seven. This off-season the money moved again: crypto out in Philadelphia, energy in, and an AI infrastructure company paying the top price in the league. IREN sells GPU computing power to companies building AI, so it's buying credibility with a global business audience as much as fan awareness. The Warriors' own pitch is that the patch is their most visible global platform. A team in a big market with a global fan base can charge for that reach.

The patch also matters because of what hangs off it. The big ones are rarely just a logo. They come with named arena spaces, hospitality, cardholder perks, G League and WNBA rights, content and community programs. SponsorUnited put NBA team sponsorship revenue at US$1.62 billion in 2024-25, up 8% on the year before, with jersey patch deals more than doubling. Once the NBA proved the model, the rest of American sport followed. The NHL allowed jersey patches from 2022-23, and MLB from 2023, with the San Diego Padres first to sign, with Motorola.

For Australian rights holders, the lesson is in the pricing. The NBA didn't make more inventory, it made less, then let 30 clubs compete to sell the one spot that turns up in every photo. Fewer, bigger, better-defined assets with rights bundled around them is the same playbook any club can run, whether it's a sleeve, a training top or a naming right.

What to watch next: whether IREN's reported fee becomes the new benchmark when the next big-market patch comes up, and whether AI and energy brands keep replacing the finance and crypto money that defined the first decade of patches. Watch the activation too. A patch deal that only ever shows up on the shirt is the easiest one to lose at renewal.
article.close: It's the smallest logo in the building, and the most expensive one.

features.headline: The AO's partner machine.
features.descriptor: Why the Australian Open keeps signing new brands

article.standfirst: Three deals in eight days, with AO 2027 less than three months away. Tennis Australia has turned sponsorship into a production line.
body: In the space of eight days this month, Tennis Australia signed DoorDash as the Australian Open's official on-demand delivery partner, named Adobe its official AI marketing and creativity partner, and locked Sky in as the tournament's New Zealand broadcaster through to 2032. Nobody put a number on any of the three. Together they show how the AO makes its money now: keep building new things to sell, then carve them into very specific categories.

Start with the categories. A footy club has a shirt front, a sleeve and some signage to flog. The AO's partner list reads more like a shopping centre directory. Kia has been the major partner since 2002. Emirates, Rolex and Luzhou Laojiao sit at associate level, with the Chinese baijiu maker on board since 2019. Below them runs a long tail of tightly defined deals: ANZ as official bank, Altos as official tequila in its Grand Slam debut, DiDi as ride share partner for AO 2026, and now DoorDash for delivery and Adobe for AI marketing. Because the deals are sold by category, every new category is extra money rather than a discount on an old one.

The bigger trick is making more event to sell. The AO now runs over three weeks, with an Opening Week in front of the main draw. In 2026 total attendance hit a record 1,368,043, up from 1,218,831 the year before. Opening Week alone pulled 217,999, nearly double 2025, on the back of open practice sessions, the first Opening Ceremony and the AO 1 Point Slam. Crowds also cracked 100,000 on four separate days for the first time. More days with people through the gates means more days a partner can activate, and the AO LIVE concerts, which ran five nights at John Cain Arena in 2026, stretch the precinct into the evening too.

The 1 Point Slam is the best example of inventory built from scratch. Amateurs and pros play single-point matches for a winner-takes-all $1 million. In January it ran on Rod Laver Arena as the AO 1 Point Slam Driven by Kia, and Jordan Smith, a 29-year-old NSW state champion, knocked out Jannik Sinner on his way to the cheque. For 2027 Haier has taken the sponsorship and the format has been pushed into clubs and schools around the country. Community winners feed into state championships in December, state winners play during Opening Week, and the champion's club gets a $50,000 grant. One property now gives a sponsor a grassroots program and a primetime moment.

The media money underwrites the lot. Nine holds the AO and the summer of tennis from 2025 to 2029 in a deal Nine said carried a $425 million cash component, the biggest in Tennis Australia's history. Australians watched 149 million hours of the 2025 tournament across platforms, up 8 per cent, and the 2026 prize pool climbed 16 per cent to a record $111.5 million. Those audiences are what partners are really buying.

This month's deals show where the next dollar comes from. The Sky renewal adds New Zealand rights to the Laver Cup and United Cup, keeps every main draw match live on Sky's platforms and puts evening sessions on free-to-air Three and ThreeNow from 2027, extending a 25-year relationship. Adobe is a different beast. It's the software giant's first tennis sponsorship anywhere, and Tennis Australia will use Adobe CX Enterprise to show each fan the matches, food and activities most relevant to them. DoorDash plays the same game at the bar: from AO 2027, patrons at the Golden Hour Bar on Grand Slam Oval can order from selected vendors through DoorDash, an AO first. The partner becomes part of the plumbing, and the event runs better for it.

For rights holders the lesson travels well beyond Melbourne Park. The AO didn't sit around waiting for brands to want a bigger logo. It built new inventory, from Opening Week to a concert series to a $1 million novelty event, and gave partners a job inside it. For brands, the open door is the category list. If there's room for an official tequila and an official AI marketing partner, there's room for plenty more.
article.close: AO 2027 runs 11 to 31 January. Watch whether Opening Week grows again, and how many more 'official' partners land before the first ball.
